html:
The Manila galleons were Spanish trading ships that sailed once or twice a year across the Pacific between Manila in the Philippines and Acapulco in Mexico, from 1565 to 1815. They made the first lasting trade link between Asia and the Americas.

The route depended on a discovery by the friar and navigator Andrés de Urdaneta in 1565: sailing east from the Philippines, ships had to go far north to catch westerly winds across to California. The eastward voyage took four to six months and was one of the hardest at sea.

The trade was simple. Silver from the mines of New Spain and Potosí went west; Chinese silk, porcelain and other goods, brought to Manila by Chinese junks, went east. Ming China, which taxed in silver, absorbed huge amounts of it. Historians count this as the moment a truly global trade began. Crops crossed too: maize and the sweet potato reached Asia this way; see Sweet potato reaches China. The galleons ended when Mexico's war of independence cut the route; see also Manila galleon trade.
